video_title: Why the Next Generation of Enterprise Software Looks Nothing Like Salesforce
gist: Keith Paris, CEO of Lightfield, tells a16z partners how he shut down Tome (an AI presentation product at roughly 2 million users a month) and rebuilt a CRM as a 'business world model' founded on a chronological activity log instead of a predefined schema. The conversation is an operating manual on cold-start distribution (free office space as 'negative pricing'), the greenfield-to-brownfield wedge against Salesforce, a three-part pricing architecture adopted after both pure seat and pure consumption pricing failed, and running a 40-person company with no functional swim lanes.

themes.theme: Killing Tome and cold-starting a CRM

insights.claim: Tome, an AI presentation product that launched around the time of ChatGPT, reached roughly 2 million users a month and about 25 million cumulative users, and its founders shut it down anyway because none of them liked the product they had built.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Raw consumer usage growth in AI-native apps can coexist with zero founder conviction; user counts are a weak signal of durable value in the LLM-wrapper category.
insights.quote: none of us like the product which is which is kind of a funny thing to say.

insights.claim: The binding constraint on AI-generated presentations was missing context about the presenter, the audience and their relationship, not model reasoning ability, which is why the team refused to shrink and wait out the capability curve from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A test for AI application investments: when the gap is context rather than reasoning, scaling laws will not rescue the product, and the defensible business belongs to whoever assembles the context.
insights.quote: the model just didn't have enough context to to really understand the presenter, the audience, the relationship between the presenter and the audience and like no amount of general reasoning gets you past that.

insights.claim: Lightfield found its B2B direction by mining Tome's own user base, discovering the business users were sales and marketing, then running 12 free pilots with companies of roughly 500,000 people and following the requests that came back for research, lead qualification and expansion analysis.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A repeatable pivot playbook: harvest the dying product's user base as free distribution for demand discovery instead of starting cold.
insights.quote: I think what makes early stage founders good at this is that you you sort of have no priors.

insights.claim: When Lightfield asked customers for access to Salesforce, call recorders and data warehouses in order to do work for them, it found the data incomplete and conflicting — the call recorder frequently disagreed with the CRM — and concluded that reorganizing that reality for machines and humans was the more enduring business.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Identifies the real bottleneck in the AI go-to-market stack as data reconciliation rather than agent execution, which is where durable margin is likely to sit.
insights.quote: what the the call recorder often had a different view of reality than the CRM.

insights.claim: Lightfield's first attempt, a go-to-market assistant, had daily users but could not be monetized because the company had no pricing power over data it did not own and ten competitors were selling the same layer.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Direct warning on the AI-assistant category: owning the system of record, not the workflow layer above it, is what creates pricing power.
insights.quote: we had all of these AES using it every day but we had no pricing power because it wasn't our data.

insights.claim: After rebuilding a CRM from first principles in the dark for four months, Lightfield could not get anyone to adopt it and bootstrapped its first ten customers by offering free space in the office it could not get rid of in exchange for using the product.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A concrete template for solving cold start in a system-of-record category where switching cost, not product quality, is the barrier.
insights.quote: I'm gonna post on X and LinkedIn. You can sit in our office space if you use our CRM.

insights.claim: The signal that the new CRM was working was intensity rather than satisfaction: ten startups used a slow, incomplete product every day and sent Slack complaints roughly every two hours, in sharp contrast with Tome's large but passive user base.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: An early-stage product-market-fit metric worth borrowing: hourly unsolicited complaint volume beats scale as an indicator of indispensability.

insights.claim: Three of Lightfield's five founding members came from Facebook, and they modeled the CRM on the Facebook timeline — building a chronological activity log of every outreach, reply, meeting, document exchange, product usage event and payment as the canonical record, with conventional CRM fields and stages derived from it.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: The architectural bet that separates this from incumbent CRMs: fields become a derived view, so a changed data model can be backfilled from the log rather than lost forever.

insights.claim: Lightfield tried a fully unstructured store and abandoned it because queries took too long and hit needle-in-a-haystack retrieval problems, settling on a semi-structured design that holds large volumes of unstructured data inside the activity log for the system to infer causality from.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A practical counterexample to the 'dump everything into a vector store' architectures now common in AI enterprise products.
insights.quote: we we actually tried going fully unstructured.

insights.claim: CRM consultants told Lightfield their most consequential contribution is the customer's data model, and that a wrong model is unrecoverable because reps will never go back in time to fill in fields — which is why Lightfield made onboarding effectively schemaless, connecting email, a call recorder and a data warehouse and assembling relationships in real time.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Names the incumbent failure mode that creates the opening: implementation and modeling risk, not feature gaps, is what makes traditional CRM deployments fail.
insights.quote: the biggest most consequential decision they help you with is your your data model.

insights.claim: Lightfield's organizing principle is that intelligence substitutes for schema, turning setup into a consumer-style flow where the user presses sync, waits about five minutes and has an assembled model of their business.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: If schema definition is the real cost of enterprise software, the attack surface against incumbents is implementation time — and consulting-heavy revenue pools are exposed.
insights.quote: basically like intelligence is greater than schema.

insights.claim: Arbitrary custom objects and relationships let a company called Power model both a B2B pharmaceutical business and a consumer patient marketplace, scrape the FDA and clinicaltrials.gov into a world model of every trial underway, and match patients to trials and sponsors.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Shows arbitrary-schema systems of record being repurposed as vertical matching engines, expanding the addressable market well beyond conventional sales teams.
insights.quote: Lightfield actually helped someone with Alzheimer's find frontier treatment within days.

insights.claim: The brownfield problem in enterprise software is that incumbents hold hostages rather than customers, so a strictly better product is insufficient to displace them — historical breaks such as on-premise to cloud worked by redefining the problem rather than winning feature-for-feature.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Sets the bar for AI-native application startups: category redefinition, not a better version of the category, is what unseats entrenched enterprise vendors.
insights.quote: the best companies have hostages not customers like SAP has hostages

insights.claim: Lightfield deliberately targeted brand-new companies through LinkedIn prospecting and cold emails to YC startups, and that base compounds unusually fast right now — customers that joined with zero reps now have around 100 reps, compressing years of enterprise learning into months.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A reason to re-rate startup-focused SaaS: faster customer graduation converts a low-ACV base into enterprise ACV inside a normal fund cycle.

insights.claim: Lightfield's contrarian bet is that the wedge into incumbent accounts is helping leaders understand and steer a chaotic company, not the 'do the work' automation — lead scoring and outbound email — advertised on every AI CRM billboard in Silicon Valley, because Salesforce can simply ship that.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: If correct, AI-SDR and outbound-automation startups are competing in exactly the layer incumbents absorb most easily, while understanding and forecasting is the defensible ground.

insights.claim: Lightfield gives its product away free to everyone in a customer's company on sales-led plans, deliberately building company-wide dependencies across engineering, support and finance so an incoming Salesforce-trained VP of sales faces internal resistance instead of being able to rip and replace.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A concrete defense against the well-known pattern where a newly hired sales executive reverts the stack to the incumbent they were trained on.
insights.quote: it'll create sort of real company network effects that make it harder to rip and replace us.

insights.claim: Lightfield chose pragmatism over AI purism — keeping dashboards, tables and spreadsheet views, which the CEO himself uses to run sales meetings, while offering chat, MCP and CLI for frontier users — on the view that deterministic dashboards remain an unwon war because people want the same view every morning with their coffee.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Tempers the thesis that conversational interfaces replace BI; the recurring-glance use case is a durable product requirement and likely a durable category.
insights.quote: we haven't won the war on uh you know deterministic dashboards.

insights.claim: Lightfield replaced the classic sales sequence builder of arrows, conditions and variables with a chat interaction in which an agent writes a recipe informed by the world model, and sales leaders who initially demanded their knobs and switches converted once they saw it was more efficient and required less learning.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A live example of the visual workflow-builder paradigm collapsing into natural language, which threatens marketing-automation tooling built on that UI.

themes.theme: Pricing after seat and credit failures

insights.claim: Lightfield began with pure seat pricing to match the Salesforce and HubSpot model and it failed on unit economics because the heaviest consumers used roughly 10,000 times more than the lightest.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Quantifies why per-seat pricing breaks for inference-heavy software — a margin risk for every incumbent SaaS vendor bolting AI onto existing seat contracts.
insights.quote: the head just the head was using 10,000x more than the tail.

insights.claim: Pure consumption pricing, with everything denominated in credits, froze customer behavior entirely — signups stopped touching the product — in what the CEO called the worst three weeks of the company's life.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Empirical evidence that metered pricing suppresses adoption in daily-use software, cutting against current enthusiasm for all-consumption AI pricing.
insights.quote: then we found that nobody touched anything.

insights.claim: Lightfield segments its work into four buckets — everyday CRM capture and record updates, pipeline generation, workflow automation, and intelligence and forecasting — charging a fixed platform fee plus seats for the first because customers refuse budget uncertainty on core CRM, and metering the rest.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A transferable hybrid pricing template for AI software: fix the price of the system of record, meter the work and the alpha.
insights.quote: I don't want to think about the like error bounds of my core CRM when I look at my budget

insights.claim: Lightfield rejected outcome-based pricing because a sales tool's outcomes depend on the customer's own product-market fit — outbound prospecting would be trivially effective for a company like OpenAI and futile for a seed-stage startup with no website — so it charges for work instead.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Explains why outcome pricing generalizes to support, a measurable cost center, but not to revenue categories where the vendor cannot control input quality.
insights.quote: we can't quite charge for the outcome in the space uh for now.

insights.claim: Seed-stage founders routinely told Lightfield they could build the same product over four weekends, and those who tried came back reporting hallucinations and bad outbound emails.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Field evidence that the 'SaaS is dead, build it yourself' thesis is overstated at the system-of-record layer, at least at current model capability.

insights.claim: Larger companies do not propose building their own system of record — they propose building their own company brain — and they return after discovering that modeling customers is the hardest part of building a business world model.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Pinpoints where internal AI platform projects fail, and therefore what a vendor must own to remain non-replicable: the customer entity model.
insights.quote: I'm going to build my own company brain

insights.claim: Customers who kept Lightfield as the system of record but built their own harness on top via MCP or CLI generally reverted within weeks because Lightfield's harness had better entity recognition, better precision and recall, and more speed.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Suggests retrieval quality, not data storage, is the moat for AI systems of record — and that full openness is a safe strategy when the harness is genuinely better.
insights.quote: after a few weeks, they almost always realize, wait a minute, your harness was actually doing quite a bit.

insights.claim: Lightfield eliminated functional swim lanes after concluding that Tome's siloed product, marketing and CS leaders slowed the company to a crawl and made pivoting impossible because the appendages were not talking to the brain.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Ties org structure directly to pivot optionality — a specific diligence question for AI-era startups that may need to re-found themselves.
insights.quote: we had a lot of people playing house

insights.claim: Lightfield runs 40 people with a single daily company standup, a stack-ranked list of the most important problems spanning delivery, engineering and customer success, continuous daily replanning, and whoever is free picking up the next problem, so engineers, designers and CSMs all run projects.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A concrete generalist operating model that only works because AI tooling lets anyone ramp on customers, the design system and task creation.
insights.quote: we have 40 people at the company. Everyone shows up to the same standup every morning.

insights.claim: Coherence in that generalist organization is maintained by weekly editing of the go-to-market roadmap against the mission plus an asymmetric quality gate — a very low bar to start a project and a high bar to ship one — enforced through company-wide bug bashes learned at Instagram.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: The missing control system for 'anyone can build anything' organizations: the constraint moves from build capacity to shipping standards and editing.
insights.quote: the bar to start a project is very low at lightfield but the bar to ship the project is pretty high

insights.claim: The CEO's biggest fear is shipping speed, citing teardown reports of companies migrating from startup CRMs back to Salesforce — including 11 Labs, which switched after waiting roughly four months for dashboards.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Names the churn mechanism for AI-native system-of-record startups: feature latency on mundane requests, not AI quality, is what sends customers back to incumbents.
insights.quote: they couldn't get that company to build dashboards fast enough

insights.claim: A CRM is characterized as harder to move off of than a bank, which makes vertical referenceability — evidence that companies that look like you already switched — the dominant purchasing factor for systems of record even though the underlying customer data is identical across industries.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Explains why go-to-market for systems of record is logo-sequencing by vertical rather than feature marketing, and why each new vertical carries a fixed entry cost.
insights.quote: your your CRM is maybe harder to move off of than your bank.

insights.claim: Lightfield wins health tech deals easily today because it signed BAAs and ran penetration testing from the start, and because its context engineering handles complex deals with around 50 stakeholders.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Early compliance spend functions as a vertical moat; startups that defer it forfeit the regulated segments where reference networks compound fastest.

insights.claim: AI is arguably overhyped inside Silicon Valley and massively underhyped everywhere else, partly because buyers outside tech tried ChatGPT once in November 2022, saw it hallucinate, and never revisited it.
insights.speaker: Alex Rampell (a16z partner)
insights.so_what: Frames the adoption gap as the largest remaining commercial opportunity and implies distribution, not model capability, is the binding constraint on AI revenue outside tech.
insights.quote: AI is almost overhyped in Silicon Valley. I don't think it is but and it's like massively underhyped outside of this little region of the world.

insights.claim: System-of-record companies take most of their revenue scale from outside the Bay Area, so Lightfield treats Valley customers — including ones that raised $200 million with only three go-to-market people — as efficient marketing capture for reference logos in manufacturing, fintech and healthcare rather than as efficient revenue capture.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: Reframes how to read a startup's Valley-heavy customer list: as vertical entry credentials, not as the addressable revenue base.
insights.quote: I just see the focus on Silicon Valley not as a not as efficient revenue capture, but actually just like efficient marketing capture

insights.claim: Lightfield prioritizes by projected three-year expansion value of an account rather than by average customer need, on the view that a red-ocean CRM market yields disappointing initial land, so it builds preferentially for its fastest-growing customers.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A prioritization rule for competitive categories where land economics are structurally unattractive and essentially all the value sits in net revenue retention.
insights.quote: as a CRM company in a red ocean space we have to be an expansion company

insights.claim: Intelligence and forecasting is described as Lightfield's least-discovered and most valuable surface — deploying frontier models against a company's own modeled reality for scenario planning — and the CEO says he changed his own sales process after letting GPT6 run on Lightfield for a couple of hours on a weekend, while one enterprise-focused customer discovered through it that it needed to build a mid-market product line.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: If scenario planning becomes the willingness-to-pay center of gravity, value shifts from workflow software toward whoever holds the complete machine-readable model of the business.

insights.claim: The advice for founders mid-pivot is that essentially all surrounding noise — office culture nostalgia, food quality, how options will be repriced — is irrelevant, and the only real tasks are finding genuine pain, building something that solves it and staying maniacally focused on customers.
insights.speaker: Keith Paris
insights.so_what: A filter for judging whether a pivoting portfolio company is managing its team's anxiety or actually relocating to real demand.
insights.quote: almost none of the noise around you matters when you're in a pivot.
